title: Consumer goods purchase: a used laptop sale

stages.title: Is this even an Article 2 transaction?
stages.facts: A buyer emails a local electronics store asking to buy a specific used laptop the store has listed for $800.
stages.question: Is a laptop "goods" under Article 2, making this a sale-of-goods transaction?

choices.label: Yes -- a laptop is a movable, identified thing, so it's "goods"
choices.outcome: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-105 defines "goods" as things movable at the time of identification to the contract -- a specific physical laptop fits this directly.

choices.label: No -- Article 2 only covers goods sold between businesses, not to an individual buyer
choices.outcome: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-105's definition of "goods" turns on what's being sold (a movable, identified thing), not on whether the buyer is a business -- nothing in the definition excludes an individual buyer.

stages.explanation: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-105: "Goods" means all things (including specially manufactured goods) which are movable at the time of identification to the contract for sale.

stages.title: Is there a binding contract?
stages.facts: The buyer's email said "I'll take it for $800." The seller never signed anything -- they just shipped the laptop the next day.
stages.question: Does a binding contract exist without a signed writing?

choices.label: Yes -- shipping the laptop is conduct showing agreement, and open/unwritten terms don't defeat formation
choices.outcome: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-204 allows a contract to be shown "in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct by both parties," and tolerates open terms if the parties intended a contract and a remedy is reasonably certain.

choices.label: No -- without a signed writing covering every term, there's no contract yet
choices.outcome: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-204 explicitly rejects this: a sale-of-goods contract can be shown by conduct, and doesn't fail for indefiniteness merely because some terms were left open.

stages.explanation: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-204: a contract for sale of goods may be made in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct by both parties which recognizes the existence of such a contract.

changed_fact_variants.changed_fact: What if, instead of just shipping, the seller had replied with a written confirmation adding a new term -- "all sales final, no returns" -- and both the buyer and seller are merchants dealing in goods of this kind?
changed_fact_variants.effect: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-206 treats a seasonable expression of acceptance as an acceptance even with additional terms; Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-207 then asks whether that new term became part of the contract -- between merchants it does, UNLESS the offer expressly limited acceptance to its own terms, the new term materially alters the deal (a no-returns clause plausibly would), or the buyer objects within a reasonable time.

stages.title: What protections come with the purchase?
stages.facts: The seller is a retail electronics store that regularly buys and resells used laptops. Nothing in the listing said "as-is" or disclaimed any warranty.
stages.question: Does the buyer get any warranty protection even though nothing was promised in writing?

choices.label: Yes -- because the seller is a merchant dealing in these goods, an implied warranty of merchantability attaches automatically
choices.outcome: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-104 makes this seller a "merchant" (occupational dealing in goods of the kind); Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-314 then implies a warranty of merchantability by operation of law for a merchant-seller unless excluded/modified.

choices.label: No -- without an express written warranty, the buyer has no protection at all
choices.outcome: This misses Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-314: the warranty of merchantability is implied automatically for a merchant-seller -- the buyer doesn't need an express written warranty to get it.

stages.explanation: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-314: a warranty that the goods shall be merchantable is implied in a contract for their sale if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind.

changed_fact_variants.changed_fact: What if the seller were a private individual selling their own personal laptop, not a store?
changed_fact_variants.effect: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-314's implied warranty of merchantability requires a merchant-seller -- a private, non-merchant seller does not automatically give one. But if that private seller described the laptop's condition ("battery holds a full charge"), Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-313 can still create an express warranty from that affirmation or description, regardless of merchant status.

stages.title: The laptop arrives broken -- what now?
stages.facts: The laptop arrives and won't power on at all.
stages.question: What can the buyer do?

choices.label: Reject the goods (the whole shipment, since it's a single laptop) and pursue cover or damages
choices.outcome: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-601 lets a buyer reject the whole if the goods fail to conform to the contract; having rightfully rejected, Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-711 then lets the buyer "cover" (buy a replacement) and recover damages, or recover damages for nondelivery.

choices.label: The buyer must accept the laptop as-is and can only complain informally afterward
choices.outcome: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-601 gives the buyer a real right to reject nonconforming goods -- there is no rule requiring acceptance of defective goods with only an informal complaint as recourse.

stages.explanation: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-601: if the goods fail to conform to the contract, the buyer may reject the whole. Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-711: on rightful rejection, the buyer may "cover" and recover damages, or recover damages for nondelivery.

changed_fact_variants.changed_fact: What if the roles were reversed -- the laptop arrived in perfect working order, but the buyer simply refused to pay and sent it back anyway?
changed_fact_variants.effect: Va. Code Ann. § 8.2-703 governs a wrongfully rejecting buyer: the seller may withhold delivery of any remaining goods, stop delivery by a carrier, resell and recover damages, recover damages for nonacceptance (or the price in a proper case), or cancel -- the mirror image of the buyer's remedies above.
